title: A record holiday, bought on 'pay later'

lines: what US shoppers are expected to put on 'buy now, pay later' this holiday season — a record. (Adobe)
Americans are headed for a record holiday. The National Retail Federation expects more than $1.013 trillion in US spending from Nov 1 to Dec 31.
Adobe sees a record $275.1 billion online — up 6.7% from last year's $257.8 billion.
But a record $21.3 billion of it is going on 'buy now, pay later' — splitting a purchase into installments.
Those payments don't vanish; they come due in January and February. (Adobe, Sept 2026)
Retailers and lenders book the sale now. The shopper carries the bill into the new year.
Miss an installment on many plans and late fees start — the discount quietly shrinks.
Splitting a payment isn't the same as affording it. A record on 'pay later' is really a record borrowed against next year's paycheck.
Buy-now-pay-later for gifts this year, or paying up front?

source_line: Sources: National Retail Federation, Adobe Digital Insights - Nov 2026
caption:
A record holiday is coming - and a record amount of it is going on "buy now, pay later."

The National Retail Federation expects US shoppers to spend more than $1.013 trillion this holiday season (Nov 1-Dec 31, 2026). Adobe sees a record $275.1 billion online, up 6.7% from last year's $257.8 billion. But a record $21.3 billion of that is forecast to go on buy-now-pay-later plans - purchases split into installments that come due in January and February (Adobe, Sept 2026).

The sale is booked now; the bill lands in the new year. On many plans, a missed installment starts late fees - so the "deal" can quietly shrink.

My take: splitting a payment isn't the same as affording it. A record on "pay later" is really a record borrowed against next year's paycheck.

Are you putting holiday gifts on buy-now-pay-later this year, or paying up front? 👇
